questions.stem: A 23 year old man has had recurrent headaches for 2 years, about once a month. Each is a right-sided pulsating pain lasting about 12 hours, with nausea, and he lies in a dark quiet room until it passes. Walking makes it worse. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal. His BP is 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4 to 72 hours with nausea, photophobia, phonophobia and worsening with movement is migraine.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: right-sided pulsating pain lasting about 12 hours
steps.x: Unilateral, throbbing, hours long, with nausea and light and noise sensitivity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Migraine without aura.

elim: Attacks last 15 minutes to 3 hours with eye watering and restlessness.
Usually obese women with papilloedema and positional headache.
Facial pain with nasal symptoms, not recurrent monthly attacks.
Bilateral pressing pain, not worsened by activity and without nausea.

steps.x: C. Migraine without aura. Migraine: unilateral throbbing, 4 to 72 hours, nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, worse with movement.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has had three episodes over 6 months in which she cannot find her words for about 25 minutes. Each time her speech returns fully and is followed by a left-sided throbbing headache with nausea lasting most of the day. Between episodes she is well and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Aura can be visual, sensory or speech disturbance; it is fully reversible, comes before the headache, and the examination is normal between attacks.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: cannot find her words for about 25 minutes
followed by a left-sided throbbing headache
steps.x: Reversible speech disturbance, then a migrainous headache.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Migraine with aura.

elim: Usually lasts seconds to a couple of minutes with positive motor or sensory features.
A single sudden severe headache, not recurrent stereotyped attacks.
No aura and no nausea.
Sudden negative symptoms without a following headache, in an older patient with vascular risk.

steps.x: B. Migraine with aura. Aura (visual, sensory or speech) is fully reversible and precedes the headache.

questions.stem: A 34 year old accountant has migraine without aura. Her diary shows attacks almost every Saturday morning. During the week she wakes at 6 am; at weekends she sleeps until 11 am. She does not drink alcohol, rarely eats chocolate or cheese and does not take the pill.
questions.q: Which is the most likely trigger for her attacks?
questions.e: Lie-ins are one of the CHOCOLATE triggers (chocolate, hangovers, orgasms, cheese and caffeine, oral contraceptives, lie-ins, alcohol, travel, exercise).

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely trigger for her attacks?
A weekend pattern with a change in sleep.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lie-ins.

elim: She does not drink.
She rarely eats it.
She rarely eats it.
She does not take it.

steps.x: E. Weekend lie-ins. Migraine triggers: CHOCOLATE, including lie-ins.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl has had four headaches in the last month, during her exam revision when she has been sleeping about 5 hours a night. Each is throbbing, on one side, with vomiting and dislike of light, lasting most of a day. Her mother has similar headaches. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which factor is most likely to be precipitating her attacks?
questions.e: Sleep deprivation and family history are risk factors for migraine; her attacks have started with poor sleep.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which factor is most likely to be precipitating her attacks?
New attacks with short sleep, plus family history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sleep deprivation.

elim: Not mentioned in her history.
A differential with papilloedema, not a precipitant.
Not a migraine trigger in a teenager with no other features.
Causes mild frontal eye-strain headache, not vomiting and photophobia.

steps.x: E. Sleep deprivation. Migraine risk factors: sleep deprivation, family history, hormonal change.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman is 26 weeks pregnant. She has had five headaches in a month, each a one-sided throbbing pain with nausea and photophobia that settles within a day. She is well between attacks. Her BP is 116/72 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Migraine is common in pregnancy with hormonal fluctuation, especially in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: one-sided throbbing pain with nausea and photophobia
steps.x: Typical migraine features with normal BP, urine and fundi.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Migraine without aura.

elim: A persistent, progressive headache, often with papilloedema or seizures.
Fundoscopy is normal.
BP and urinalysis are normal.
Bilateral pressing pain without nausea or photophobia.

steps.x: C. Migraine without aura. Migraine is common in pregnancy; always exclude pre-eclampsia (BP and urine).

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has migraine with visual aura about twice a month. She is a non-smoker with a BMI of 23 kg/m² and BP of 118/74 mmHg. She asks her GP to start the combined oral contraceptive pill, which her sister uses.
questions.q: Which is the main risk of the combined pill for her?
questions.e: The combined pill is contraindicated in migraine because it significantly increases the risk of stroke.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the main risk of the combined pill for her?
Migraine (especially with aura) plus oestrogen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stroke.

elim: A small risk with the pill, but not the reason it is contraindicated here.
Benign, not a reason to withhold it.
Can rise on the pill, but her BP is normal and this is not the main concern.
Not supported by good evidence and not dangerous.

steps.x: D. Ischaemic stroke. Migraine: avoid the combined pill because of stroke risk.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m² has 3 months of headaches. She has previously had migraine. Her GP is concerned that the new headaches may have a different cause and lists the features that would point to idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
questions.q: Which feature would most suggest idiopathic intracranial hypertension rather than migraine?
o: Headache worse on lying down with papilloedema
questions.e: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is the key differential, especially with atypical features such as a positional headache and papilloedema in an obese woman.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which feature would most suggest idiopathic intracranial hypertension rather than migraine?
An overweight young woman with new headaches.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Positional headache with papilloedema.

elim: Common in migraine.
Typical of migraine.
Typical of migraine.
A typical migraine aura.

steps.x: A. Headache worse on lying down with papilloedema. Atypical (positional) headache in an obese woman: think IIH, check fundi.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has had migraine with aura since his teens. He attends with a headache and says it is not like his usual attacks. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 146/90 mmHg. His doctor reviews which features would mean this is not migraine.
questions.q: Which feature would be most concerning for a secondary cause?
o: Sudden onset reaching maximum within a minute
Visual zig-zags that resolve within 30 minutes
questions.e: A sudden worst-ever headache, meningism or a persistent neurological deficit suggest a secondary cause such as subarachnoid haemorrhage and need investigation.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which feature would be most concerning for a secondary cause?
A change from the usual pattern; look for red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thunderclap onset.

elim: Common in migraine.
Typical of migraine.
Typical of migraine.
His usual aura.

steps.x: C. Sudden onset reaching maximum within a minute. Red flags: sudden worst-ever headache, meningism, persistent neurological deficit.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has recurrent headaches. He has been told they are either migraine or cluster headache. He does not smoke. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg, and neurological examination is normal between attacks. His GP asks about the timing of the attacks.
questions.q: Which feature of the history would most support migraine?
o: Attacks at the same time each night for 6 weeks
Each attack lasting about a day
Pacing around the room during attacks
Watering of one eye during attacks
questions.e: Migraine attacks typically last 4 to 72 hours and are worse with movement; cluster attacks are short, nightly and with autonomic features.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which feature of the history would most support migraine?
Duration is the key discriminator.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A day-long attack.

elim: The circadian clustering of cluster headache.
Typical cluster duration.
Restlessness is typical of cluster; migraine sufferers keep still.
An autonomic feature of cluster headache.

steps.x: C. Each attack lasting about a day. Migraine lasts 4 to 72 hours; cluster lasts 15 to 180 minutes.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has migraine with aura. She describes her aura in detail to a neurologist. Her neurological examination between attacks is normal. The neurologist considers which description best fits a typical migraine aura rather than a vascular event.
questions.q: Which description of the aura is most typical of migraine?
o: Flashing lights that spread over 20 minutes and fully resolve
Loss of vision in one eye like a curtain
Sudden loss of the right half of the visual field lasting 2 minutes
Visual loss on standing up quickly
Weakness of one arm that persists for 3 days
questions.e: Migraine aura is positive (zig-zags, flashing lights), develops gradually, lasts minutes and is fully reversible.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which description of the aura is most typical of migraine?
Positive, spreading and fully reversible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Spreading flashing lights that resolve.

elim: Amaurosis fugax, a carotid TIA.
Sudden negative symptoms suggest TIA.
A persistent deficit is not aura; think stroke.
A postural or IIH-related symptom.

steps.x: A. Flashing lights that spread over 20 minutes and fully resolve. Migraine aura: positive, gradual spread, under an hour, fully reversible.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman attends the emergency department with a migraine and vomiting. She is given intravenous metoclopramide. Two hours later her eyes are fixed looking upwards and her neck is twisted to one side. She is alert. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
questions.e: Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are dopamine antagonists that can cause extrapyramidal side effects, more common in young people and females.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
A young woman given a dopamine antagonist.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute dystonia from metoclopramide.

elim: She is alert with sustained postures after a dopamine antagonist.
Causes weakness, not oculogyric crisis.
She is afebrile, and neck twisting is not neck stiffness.
Causes agitation, hyperthermia and clonus.

steps.x: A. Acute dystonic reaction to metoclopramide. Dopamine antagonist antiemetics can cause dystonia, especially in young females.

questions.stem: A 21 year old student has had episodic left-sided throbbing headaches with photophobia and nausea for 3 years, each lasting about 8 hours. Neurological examination, fundoscopy and BP are normal. She has read online that headaches can be due to brain tumours and asks for a scan.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis; no routine imaging is needed unless red flags are present.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
Long stable history, typical features, normal examination.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No investigation.

elim: Not indicated without red flags.
Not used to diagnose migraine.
For suspected meningitis, SAH or IIH.
Not indicated without red flags; reassurance is appropriate.

steps.x: E. No investigation required. Migraine: clinical diagnosis; image only with red flags.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with migraine developed a sudden severe occipital headache while lifting a box 2 hours ago. She says it is the worst headache of her life and unlike her migraines. She has vomited twice and has neck stiffness. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 64 bpm and BP 168/96 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Red flags (sudden worst-ever headache and meningism) mean investigating for a secondary cause; urgent non-contrast CT is first.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Thunderclap headache with meningism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent non-contrast CT head.

elim: For giant cell arteritis in over-50s.
Done after a CT, and only if the CT is negative and over 12 hours have passed.
Not the first test for suspected bleeding.
She has red flags for a secondary cause.

steps.x: E. Non-contrast CT head. Migraine is not investigated, unless red flags: then image.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has migraine with aura. Three days ago his usual tingling in the left hand came on, followed by a headache. The headache has settled, but the tingling and weakness of his left hand are still present today. His pulse rate is 76 bpm, regular, and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Aura is fully reversible; a persistent neurological deficit is a red flag and needs brain imaging for a secondary cause such as stroke.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
The aura has not resolved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Brain imaging.

elim: Does not show stroke.
Fine for typical migraine, not for a persistent deficit.
A persistent deficit is a red flag.
For peripheral neuropathy, not a deficit following aura.

steps.x: E. Urgent MRI brain. Aura that does not fully resolve = red flag: image the brain.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with a BMI of 34 kg/m² has 2 months of daily headaches she thinks are migraine. They are worse in the morning and on bending. She has occasional blurred vision lasting seconds. Her BP is 124/80 mmHg and neurological examination is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial examination before diagnosing migraine?
questions.e: Positional headache and visual obscurations in an obese woman suggest idiopathic intracranial hypertension, the key differential; fundoscopy looks for papilloedema.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate initial examination before diagnosing migraine?

clues: worse in the morning and on bending
steps.x: Atypical positional features in an obese woman.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fundoscopy for papilloedema.

elim: Assesses the ear, not intracranial pressure.
For giant cell arteritis in people over 50.
Assesses proprioception, not raised pressure.
Will not show papilloedema.

steps.x: A. Fundoscopy. Before calling it migraine, look at the fundi if features are atypical.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has migraine with aura. She has been prescribed oral sumatriptan with ibuprofen. Each attack starts with 30 minutes of flashing lights followed by a throbbing headache. She asks when she should take the sumatriptan.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Take it as soon as the aura begins
Take it daily to prevent attacks
Take it once the headache starts
Take it only if the headache lasts over 24 hours
Take it the evening before likely attacks
questions.e: Sumatriptan is taken once the headache starts, not during the aura phase.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: flashing lights followed by a throbbing headache
when she should take the sumatriptan
steps.x: She has aura then headache.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: At headache onset.

elim: Triptans are taken at headache onset, not during aura.
Triptans are acute treatments, and daily use risks medication overuse headache.
Delay reduces effectiveness.
Not how triptans are used.

steps.x: C. Take it once the headache starts. Triptans: at headache onset, after the aura.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had migraine without aura for many years. He had a myocardial infarction 1 year ago and has stable angina. His attacks happen twice a month and last a day. His BP is 128/78 mmHg. His previous GP prescribed sumatriptan.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate acute treatment?
questions.e: Triptans are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, previous MI, stroke, peripheral vascular disease and hypertension, so simple analgesia is used.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate acute treatment?
Coronary disease rules out triptans.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Simple analgesia: paracetamol.

elim: A vasoconstrictor, contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease.
Contraindicated after MI and in ischaemic heart disease.
All triptans share the contraindication.
A different route, but still a triptan.

steps.x: D. Paracetamol 1 g. Triptan contraindications: IHD, MI, stroke, PVD, hypertension.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with migraine without aura takes oral sumatriptan with ibuprofen at the start of each headache. This helps her pain, but she has severe nausea with every attack and sometimes vomits after an hour. She has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
questions.e: Nausea and vomiting in migraine are treated with a dopamine antagonist antiemetic such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
Her pain responds; nausea is the problem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add an antiemetic: metoclopramide.

elim: A prophylactic drug for frequent attacks, not for nausea.
Opioids worsen nausea and risk medication overuse headache.
No role in migraine-related nausea.
Prophylaxis, not acute nausea.

steps.x: D. Metoclopramide. Migraine nausea: metoclopramide or prochlorperazine (watch for extrapyramidal effects).

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman is 20 weeks pregnant. She has a migraine attack with unilateral throbbing headache and photophobia, which is typical of her usual attacks. Her BP is 112/70 mmHg and urinalysis is normal. She asks what she can take for the attack.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: In pregnancy and breastfeeding, paracetamol is the first-line acute treatment for migraine.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
A pregnant woman with a typical migraine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Paracetamol.

elim: High-dose aspirin is avoided in pregnancy.
Opioids are avoided where possible and risk overuse headache.
NSAIDs are avoided, especially in the third trimester.
Teratogenic prophylaxis, not acute treatment.

steps.x: D. Paracetamol. Migraine in pregnancy: paracetamol first.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has migraine without aura. Oral sumatriptan and then oral rizatriptan, each combined with ibuprofen, have not relieved her attacks. Paracetamol and aspirin alone also did not help. She has no cardiovascular disease. Her BP is 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate acute treatment?
questions.e: When at least two triptans have failed and over-the-counter analgesia is ineffective, the CGRP antagonist rimegepant is used for acute attacks (NICE).

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate acute treatment?
Two triptans and simple analgesia have failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rimegepant.

elim: Opioids are not recommended for migraine.
Not recommended; vasoconstrictive side effects.
A prophylactic drug, not an acute treatment.
A third triptan is unlikely to help after two have failed and NICE then recommends rimegepant.

steps.x: D. Rimegepant. Two triptans failed: rimegepant (CGRP inhibitor).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has migraine without aura with six disabling attacks a month despite optimal acute treatment. She has no asthma, diabetes or Raynaud's phenomenon and is not depressed. She is sexually active and does not plan pregnancy at present. Her BP is 120/76 mmHg and pulse rate 74 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate prophylactic treatment?
questions.e: Propranolol is first-line prophylaxis when there are no contraindications; topiramate is avoided in women of childbearing age.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate prophylactic treatment?

clues: no asthma, diabetes or Raynaud's phenomenon
steps.x: Frequent attacks and no contraindication to a beta blocker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Propranolol.

elim: A second-line option.
Third-line prophylaxis.
Teratogenic and not recommended in women of childbearing age.
Teratogenic; contraindicated in women of childbearing age.

steps.x: B. Propranolol. Prophylaxis: propranolol or amitriptyline first; topiramate or candesartan second; rimegepant third.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has frequent migraine attacks needing prophylaxis. She has Raynaud's phenomenon and has had low mood and poor sleep for several months. She is not pregnant and does not have asthma or diabetes. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate prophylactic treatment?
questions.e: Amitriptyline is first-line prophylaxis and may help comorbid low mood; propranolol is avoided in Raynaud's.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate prophylactic treatment?
Propranolol is ruled out and depression favours amitriptyline.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Amitriptyline.

elim: Second-line.
Contraindicated with Raynaud's phenomenon.
Third-line.
Contraindicated in women of childbearing age.

steps.x: A. Amitriptyline. Raynaud's or asthma: avoid propranolol; amitriptyline also helps low mood.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has chronic migraine with eight attacks a month. Propranolol for 3 months did not help, and amitriptyline caused intolerable drowsiness. He has no history of kidney stones or glaucoma. His BP is 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next prophylactic treatment?
questions.e: After first-line propranolol and amitriptyline fail, second-line options are topiramate or candesartan; topiramate is suitable in a man.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate next prophylactic treatment?

clues: Propranolol for 3 months did not help
steps.x: First-line options have failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line: topiramate.

elim: Not tolerated.
An acute treatment; daily use causes medication overuse headache.
Already failed.
Third-line, after second-line drugs.

steps.x: E. Topiramate. Topiramate is second-line, not for women of childbearing age.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with migraine without aura cannot keep oral sumatriptan down because she vomits early in her attacks even after an antiemetic. She has a strong fear of needles and refuses injections. She has no cardiovascular disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral sumatriptan at a higher dose
questions.e: If oral treatment is not tolerated, nasal or subcutaneous sumatriptan is used; she declines needles so the nasal route is best.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Oral route fails; injections declined.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Nasal sumatriptan.

elim: Another oral drug she will vomit up.
Will still be vomited.
No role in migraine.
Effective but she refuses injections.

steps.x: A. Nasal sumatriptan. Oral not tolerated: nasal or subcutaneous sumatriptan.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has migraine without aura. During an attack she has throbbing pain over her left temple. A medical student asks what is happening around the brain during the attack to cause the pain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Inflammation of the temporal artery wall
questions.e: Migraine pain follows activation of the trigeminovascular system, releasing neuropeptides such as CGRP that cause neurogenic inflammation and dilation of meningeal vessels.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism?

clues: what is happening around the brain
steps.x: Pain from meningeal vessels via the trigeminal nerve.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Trigeminovascular activation and CGRP.

elim: The mechanism of IIH or mass lesions.
The old theory of tension-type headache.
Central to cluster headache.
Giant cell arteritis.

steps.x: E. Trigeminovascular activation releasing CGRP. Migraine: trigeminovascular activation, CGRP, neurogenic inflammation, meningeal vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has migraine with aura. Before each headache, tingling starts in his fingers and marches slowly up his arm to his face over 20 minutes, then fades in the same order. Neurological examination between attacks is normal.
questions.q: Which best describes the mechanism of this slowly spreading symptom?
o: A wave of depolarisation then suppressed activity across the cortex
Embolism to the middle cerebral artery
Transient demyelination of the spinal cord
questions.e: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depression: a slow wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation followed by suppressed activity spreading across the cortex.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which best describes the mechanism of this slowly spreading symptom?
A symptom that spreads slowly over minutes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cortical spreading depression.

elim: Gives sudden, not slowly spreading, deficits.
Spreads in seconds, not over 20 minutes.
Would not march from fingers to face.
Does not cause a spreading face and arm symptom.

steps.x: A. A wave of depolarisation then suppressed activity across the cortex. Aura = cortical spreading depression.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with migraine says that during attacks even brushing her hair or wearing earrings on the painful side hurts. Between attacks her scalp feels normal. Neurological examination between attacks is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this symptom?
o: Damage to the trigeminal nerve root
Sensitisation of trigeminal and central pain pathways
questions.e: Sensitisation of trigeminal nociceptors and central pain pathways causes the throbbing pain and cutaneous allodynia of migraine.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of this symptom?

clues: Between attacks her scalp feels normal
steps.x: Pain from normally harmless touch only during attacks.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Allodynia from sensitisation.

elim: Would cause constant sensory change, not attack-only pain.
A skin condition, not attack-related.
Gives constant occipital pain.
Not the mechanism of migraine.

steps.x: E. Sensitisation of trigeminal and central pain pathways. Migraine allodynia: peripheral and central sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with migraine has started having central chest tightness 20 minutes after taking oral sumatriptan. He has hypertension and smokes. An ECG during the symptoms shows ST depression in V4 to V6. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 162/98 mmHg.

visual.title: ECG during chest tightness
visual.caption: Lateral ST depression: ischaemia after a triptan.

questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his chest symptoms?
questions.e: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists causing cranial vasoconstriction; 5-HT1B receptors on coronary arteries explain why they are contraindicated in IHD and hypertension.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his chest symptoms?

clues: ST depression in V4 to V6
steps.x: Ischaemia triggered by a triptan.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coronary vasoconstriction via 5-HT1B.

elim: No rash, wheeze or hypotension.
CGRP dilates vessels; it is not caused by triptans.
The mechanism of antiemetic side effects, not triptans.
The action of SSRIs, not triptans.

steps.x: A. 5-HT1B receptor-mediated coronary vasoconstriction. Triptans = 5-HT1B/1D agonists; they constrict coronary arteries too.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman with migraine has been started on rimegepant after two triptans failed. She asks her pharmacist how the new drug works and why it is different from her old tablets.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of rimegepant?
questions.e: Rimegepant is a CGRP inhibitor; CGRP is a key mediator of the neurogenic inflammation driving migraine pain.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the mechanism of action of rimegepant?
A gepant: the name gives the target.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CGRP blockade.

elim: The action of triptans.
The action of propranolol.
The action of NSAIDs.
The action of metoclopramide and prochlorperazine.

steps.x: C. Blocking the action of CGRP. Rimegepant blocks CGRP, the key mediator of migraine neurogenic inflammation.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has had migraine for 20 years. Over 6 months her headaches have become daily and dull, present on waking. She takes sumatriptan or co-codamol on about 18 days each month. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal. Her BP is 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the change in her headaches?
questions.e: Medication overuse headache is a recognised complication of frequent acute migraine treatment, typically triptans or opioids on many days a month.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the change in her headaches?
Frequent acute medicines with a change to daily headache.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Medication overuse headache.

elim: Normal examination and fundi after 6 months make this unlikely.
Possible, but frequent analgesic use is the key clue.
Fundoscopy is normal.
Cluster does not cause daily dull headache.

steps.x: D. Medication overuse headache. Frequent acute treatment (triptans, opioids) causes medication overuse headache.
